A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system that helps websites load faster no matter where a visitor is located. Normally, every request for a photo, video, or webpage travels all the way back to a single origin server — the original computer where the website's files are permanently stored. If that server is far away, loading takes longer. A CDN solves this by placing copies of the same files on many computers scattered around the world, called edge locations, which are smaller stations positioned much closer to where people actually are. When a request arrives, it gets routed to the nearest edge location instead of the distant origin server. If that nearby location already has a saved copy of the requested file, this is called a cache hit, and the content can be delivered almost instantly without ever bothering the origin server. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries stocking popular books instead of forcing every reader to travel to one central library across the country. Only when a file is missing or outdated does the edge location have to fetch a fresh copy from the origin, store it, and then serve it locally from then on. This setup reduces waiting time, eases strain on the origin server, and keeps things running smoothly even during traffic spikes, since the workload is spread across many locations rather than piled onto one. The result is a browsing experience that feels quick and reliable, whether someone is streaming a video, reading news, or shopping online.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's true, permanent files | Every new or updated file eventually has to come from here |
| Edge location | A smaller computer positioned close to end users, holding stored copies of files | Shortens the distance data has to travel, speeding delivery up |
| Cache hit | A case where the nearby edge location already has the requested file ready | Delivers content almost instantly, without contacting the origin server |
| Cache miss | A case where the edge location does not yet have the requested file | Forces a slower trip back to the origin server before a local copy can be stored |
